questions.question: What are the most useful Hash methods in Ruby?
questions.title: Essential Ruby Hash Methods
questions.direct_answer: A Hash maps keys to values: {name: 'Ada', age: 30}. The essentials: h[:name] (lookup, nil if missing); h[:name] = 'Bob' (set); h.key?(:name) (has key?); h.value?('Ada') (has value?); h.keys / h.values (arrays of keys/values); h.each { |k,v| ... } (iterate pairs); h.map { |k,v| [k, v*2] }.to_h (transform to a new hash); h.merge(other) (combine, right wins); h.select { |k,v| v > 18 } (filter to new hash); h.delete(:age) (remove a key, returns value); h.transform_values { |v| v*2 } (map values, keep keys). Default: h = Hash.new(0) gives 0 for missing keys (great for counting: h[word] += 1). Hashes preserve insertion order in Ruby (since 1.9).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know h[:k] lookup/set, each with |k,v|, merge, transform_values, and Hash.new(0) for counting.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using h['name'] (string) when keys are symbols (:name) — returns nil. Or h.map without .to_h (returns an array of pairs, not a hash).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Hashes: h[:k] get/set, key?/value?, keys/values, each{|k,v|}, map{...}.to_h, merge, select, delete, transform_values. Hash.new(0) for counting. Insertion-ordered.

sections.title: Hash Methods
sections.content:
lookup/set, key?/value?, keys/values, each{|k,v|}, map+to_h, merge, transform_values, Hash.new(0).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  H[hash] --> L[h[:k] get/set]
  H --> E[each{|k,v|}]
  H --> M[merge: right wins]
  H --> TV[transform_values: map values]
  H --> D[Hash.new(0): counting]
```

sections.title: Hash methods
sections.content:
```ruby
h = { name: 'Ada', age: 30 }

h[:name]                    # 'Ada'  (lookup; nil if missing)
h[:name] = 'Bob'            # set
h.key?(:name)               # true (has key?)
h.value?('Ada')             # false (has value?)
h.keys                      # [:name, :age]
h.values                   # ['Bob', 30]
h.each { |k, v| puts "#{k}=#{v}" }   # iterate pairs

# Transform to a NEW hash:
h.map { |k, v| [k, v * 2] }.to_h   # {:name=>'Bob', :age=>60}
h.transform_values { |v| v * 2 }  # map values, keep keys

# Combine (right wins on conflict):
{ a: 1 }.merge({ a: 99, b: 2 })    # {a: 99, b: 2}

# Filter / delete:
h.select { |k, v| v > 18 }    # {:age=>30}
h.delete(:age)                # 30 (removes :age)

# Counting with a default:
counts = Hash.new(0)
words.each { |w| counts[w] += 1 }   # missing key -> 0 -> 1

# Insertion order preserved (Ruby 1.9+):
{ b: 1, a: 2 }.keys  # [:b, :a]  (order kept)
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Using h['name'] (string) when keys are symbols (:name) — returns nil.
h.map without .to_h — returns an array of pairs, not a hash.
Forgetting Hash.new(0) for counting (nil + 1 raises NoMethodError).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: h[:k] gets (nil if missing); h[:k] = v sets; key?/value? check membership.
keys/values return arrays; each { |k,v| } iterates pairs.
map { |k,v| [k, ...] }.to_h transforms to a new hash; transform_values maps values.
merge combines (right wins); select filters; delete removes a key (returns value).
Hash.new(0) gives a default for missing keys — great for counting; hashes are insertion-ordered.
